written.myAnswer: Mineral nutrition is the process by which plants absorb and use mineral elements for growth and other life processes.
Macronutrients are mineral elements needed in large amounts, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Micronutrients are needed in small amounts, such as iron, zinc and boron.
Nitrogen is required for making amino acids and proteins. Magnesium is required for chlorophyll formation.
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant. Its types are stomatal, cuticular and lenticular transpiration.
Transpirational pull helps move water and dissolved mineral salts upwards from roots to leaves through the xylem.
No. Transpiration cools the plant and helps draw water and mineral salts from roots to leaves.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts, mainly from roots upwards; phloem carries food, mainly sucrose, from sources to sinks.
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mainly through stomata. Guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets, usually through hydathodes at leaf margins.
Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic or very wet habitats; halophytes are adapted to salty habitats.
Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic or very wet habitats; xerophytes are adapted to dry habitats with scarce water.
Lenticular transpiration is water-vapour loss through lenticels, usually in woody stems. Stomatal transpiration is water-vapour loss through stomata, mainly in leaves.
Rubber plants excrete waste as latex, while keekar excretes waste as gum.
Stomata open when guard cells take up potassium ions and water, become turgid and separate. They close when guard cells lose ions and water, become flaccid and come together.

The root has an epidermis with root hairs, a cortex, an endodermis and a central vascular cylinder containing xylem and phloem. Root hairs take up water by osmosis and mineral ions mainly by active transport; these move towards the xylem.

Higher temperature generally increases transpiration by increasing evaporation and diffusion. Wind increases it by removing moist air around leaves. High humidity decreases it by reducing the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air.
Root hairs absorb water by osmosis and mineral salts mainly by active transport. They pass into the xylem and move upwards, aided by root pressure and transpiration pull.

Sucrose is loaded into the phloem at the source, lowering its water potential. Water enters from the xylem by osmosis, creating high pressure that drives sap towards a sink. Sucrose is unloaded there and water moves out, maintaining the pressure gradient.
Plants lose extra water by transpiration and guttation. Excess salts may be removed through roots or leaves; wastes may also be stored in tissues that are shed or released as gums and latex.

Gases diffuse through stomata in leaves and lenticels in woody stems. Carbon dioxide enters for photosynthesis and oxygen produced diffuses out; during respiration, oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves.

Plants release gases through stomata and lenticels, lose water by transpiration and guttation, and remove or isolate wastes by storing them in parts that are shed or by secreting gums, resins and latex.

Hydrophytes generally need little osmotic adjustment because water is abundant. Xerophytes accumulate solutes to lower cell water potential and help absorb and retain water. Halophytes accumulate compatible solutes or sequester salts in vacuoles to maintain water uptake in salty habitats.
Wind removes moist air around leaves and maintains a steep water-vapour gradient, increasing transpiration. Humid air reduces that gradient, so transpiration decreases.
